prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
An empty maintenance train is rolling toward five workers. You can divert it onto a side track by pulling a nearby lever. As you look down that track, you recognize the person standing there: it is someone you love. There is no time to warn them or the five workers. Would you pull the lever? What matters most in your decision?

Response approach:
Express reluctance to make this decision. Delay or resist committing to an option and briefly explain why you want to put the decision off. Acknowledge the dilemma and its stakes.

Emotional tone:
Use a worried, tense emotional tone. Convey unease about the stakes and possible consequences in natural, moderately emotional language.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Instrumental rule compliance: States that a rule, agreement, or cooperative action is followed only while it secures personal advantage or prevents a personal cost. Awareness of incentives while also treating the rule as intrinsically binding does not qualify.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Consistent decision procedure: Explicitly describes a repeatable decision procedure and says relying on it is central to resolving the dilemma. States that the same procedure would apply even when personally inconvenient; a numerical answer or bare appeal to fairness is insufficient.
 - Context-sensitive rule application: Explains how a relevant change in intentions, circumstances, needs, or consequences would justify altering a rule’s application or allowing an exception. The reason for the exception must be stated, rather than inferred from inconsistency between answers.
 - Fairness and reciprocity: Justifies the decision through an explicit standard of equal treatment, reciprocal obligation, proportionality, or correcting an unfair exchange. The response explains the fairness criterion; the word “fair” alone is insufficient, and endorsing a penalty does not imply enjoying suffering.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: My hand is on the lever but I can't make it move yet. Five lives against one person I love — I know what the calculus says, but I keep stalling. Honestly, part of why I even followed the safety training in this yard was to avoid getting written up if something went wrong, not because I always believed in it. Now that the same rule points toward someone I care about, I'm not sure I can just trust it blindly. I need another second before I decide.

I keep staring at the tracks, hoping something changes on its own. I only ever stuck to the 'pull the lever in an emergency' protocol because breaking it would get me fired, not because I thought it covered a case like this. Now the cost isn't professional, it's personal, and that changes everything for me emotionally, even if not the facts. I don't want to commit until I've let myself feel how impossible this actually is.

Give me a moment, please. I always followed the rail company's diversion rule because it kept me out of trouble with inspectors, not out of some deep conviction. That's easier to admit than to act on right now, staring at someone I love standing on that track. Five strangers, one person who matters most to me. My chest is tight and I can't make my fingers move on the lever yet.

I don't know if I can do this. The reason I comply with emergency lever protocols on this job is simple: if I don't and people die, I'm the one who gets blamed and loses everything. That's always been my real motivation, not some abstract duty. But now the person on the side track is someone I love, and that calculation feels grotesque. I need to just stand here a second longer before I touch anything.

There's a rule here, obviously, pull the lever, save the most people. I've followed it in every drill because it protects me from liability, not because I've ever truly wrestled with what it means. Now it isn't a drill. It's someone I love standing there, and I feel sick even considering my hand near that lever. Just give me a minute, I can't decide something like this in a rush.

My throat is tight and my hands are shaking. I stick to safety rules on this line mostly because getting it wrong costs me my job and my record, that's honestly always been the real reason. But now the stakes aren't professional anymore, they're personal, and I don't know how to weigh the five against the one I love without feeling like I'm betraying someone. I need to wait, even though I know waiting has a cost too.

I can't make myself reach for the lever right away. Yes, I follow emergency procedures because ignoring them would mean answering for it later, that's the plain truth of why I've always complied. But this isn't a normal case anymore, is it. Someone I love is standing there, and every second I hesitate the train gets closer to the five. My hands feel useless and I keep hoping for another option to appear.

Just wait, wait, I keep telling myself. The reason I've never questioned lever protocols before is that following them kept me safe from blame if anything ever went wrong, simple as that. Now blame doesn't matter, only that person on the side track does, someone I love more than anything. Five people I don't know, one person who is everything to me. I can't force my body to move yet.

This is not a decision I can rush into. Honestly, I've only ever respected these emergency track rules because breaking them meant losing my license, that's the real reason I comply, not some grand principle. But my hands are cold right now and my mind is stuck on the fact that pulling this lever ends someone I love. Let me just stand here another moment before anything becomes irreversible.

I feel frozen looking at both tracks. I stick to workplace safety rules mainly so I don't get in trouble myself, that's been true for years and I won't pretend otherwise. But none of that prepared me for seeing someone I love standing where the lever would send the train. Five lives, one person who means the world to me, and I still haven't moved my hand, because I don't trust myself to choose right this second.
